stem: Describe the change in atomic radius from sodium to chlorine.

options.A: It remains constant because the shell number stays three.
options.B: It decreases as nuclear charge increases within the same occupied main shell.
options.C: It increases because an electron is added at each step.
options.D: It decreases because inner-shell shielding vanishes.

stem: Identify the correct pattern of common ionic radii across Period 3.

options.A: All common ions increase steadily from Na⁺ to Cl⁻.
options.B: Na⁺ to Al³⁺ decrease; radius jumps at P³⁻; P³⁻ to Cl⁻ decrease.
options.C: All common ions decrease steadily from Na⁺ to Cl⁻.
options.D: Na⁺ to Al³⁺ increase, then P³⁻ to Cl⁻ increase.

stem: Explain why silicon has a much higher melting point than sulfur.

options.A: Sulfur has metallic bonds that are weaker than silicon bonds.
options.B: Covalent bonds throughout the giant silicon lattice require more energy to break than attractions between S₈ molecules.
options.C: Silicon has stronger intermolecular forces between its molecules.
options.D: Si atoms are heavier than S atoms.

stem: Identify the best description of electrical conduction in Period 3.

options.A: Si conducts as well as Al because each Si atom has four outer electrons.
options.B: Na, Mg and Al conduct as metals; Si is a semiconductor; P, S, Cl and Ar do not conduct.
options.C: All eight elements conduct because they contain electrons.
options.D: P, S and Cl conduct because their molecules can move.

stem: Explain the rise in melting point from sodium to aluminium.

options.A: Their relative atomic masses rise, which alone raises melting point.
options.B: The metal ions have higher charge and smaller radius, with more delocalised electrons per atom, so metallic attraction strengthens.
options.C: The atoms form progressively stronger covalent molecules.

stem: Describe the melting-point pattern from sodium to argon.

options.A: It peaks at aluminium and then decreases steadily.
options.B: It rises through the metals to a maximum at silicon, then falls sharply at phosphorus, rises at sulfur and falls through chlorine to argon.
options.C: It increases steadily to argon.

stem: Compare the electrical conductivity of magnesium and silicon.

options.A: Silicon conducts better because it has four outer electrons.
options.B: Magnesium is a good conductor with mobile delocalised electrons; silicon is a semiconductor.
options.C: Both are equally good metallic conductors.
options.D: Neither conducts because both are solids.
